query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, brittle behavior emerges not from bulk intermetallic precipitation but from stress- and temperature‐induced local compositional partitioning that promotes nanoscale segregation at grain boundaries. Such segregation weakens intergranular cohesion, leading to reduced toughness when the alloy is exposed to service conditions, unlike conventional alloys where preexistent grain-boundary phases dominate.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with uniform elemental distribution and no detectable grain-boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical loading combined with elevated-temperature thermal cycling to mimic aggressive service conditions relative to a control maintained at lower temperatures and reduced strain rates.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant conditions with high temperature and strain rate (or sustained loading) contrasted against baseline conditions (ambient or lower temperature, lower strain rate) to isolate the effects of stress-induced segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions where nanoscale segregation of one or more alloying elements might occur.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature and high-strain conditions, local diffusional processes promote modest but critical segregation of certain constituent elements to grain boundaries. This segregation reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries, leading to a transition from ductile to brittle fracture mechanisms even in the absence of conventional intermetallic precipitates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial homogeneous state, samples exposed to high-temperature thermal cycling and mechanical loading will exhibit localized grain-boundary compositional fluctuations as detected by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM, along with measurable reductions in fracture toughness. The control condition should retain uniform composition and high toughness.
generation.baseline: The initial fully homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy state with high ductility and fracture resistance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies primarily under service or loading conditions where sufficient thermal activation and mechanical stress promote local segregation without triggering full-scale phase decomposition or grain coarsening. Outside these conditions (e.g., at lower temperatures or strain rates), the alloy retains its toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of toughness degradation attributable solely to nanoscale grain-boundary segregation and its competition with other potential decohesion mechanisms remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase HEA specimens: one subjected to aggressive loading (high temperature and strain rate/thermal cycling) and one maintained under controlled, benign conditions. Analyze both sets using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM for evidence of grain-boundary segregation, and perform standardized fracture toughness tests.
measurements: Atom probe tomography to quantify elemental segregation at grain boundaries
Transmission electron microscopy to observe nanoscale segregation features
Fracture toughness or bend tests to measure mechanical performance degradation
EBSD to confirm that no significant grain-coarsening (or phase transformation) occurs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aggressively loaded samples do not show statistically significant grain-boundary compositional segregation and corresponding reduction in fracture toughness relative to the control samples, or if toughness degradation occurs via a different microstructural pathway (e.g., grain coarsening or formation of intermetallic phases), then the hypothesis that stress-induced segregation governs the emergence of brittleness in the HEA is falsified.
